title: Persisting When It's Hard
keyIdea: Hard things get easier when you keep trying. A mistake is a clue that shows what to change, so try a different way instead of the same way again. Say "I can't do it yet", take a calm break if you feel cross, then have another go.

kid: Some things are hard. That is OK. Hard means you are learning.
A mistake is a clue. If your throw is too short, throw a bit harder next time. Try a new way. The same try gives the same result.
Say "I can't do it yet." The word yet means you will get there.
Feel cross? Take a break. Breathe in and out. Then try again.
adult: Persistence at this age means staying with a tricky task, treating a mistake as information and trying a different approach rather than repeating the same move or giving up. The English early years framework lists it as a characteristic of effective learning: keeping on trying when challenges occur and bouncing back after difficulties.

Two ideas help five- and six-year-olds most. First, a mistake tells you what to change: too short means harder, a tower that falls means a different order. Second, skills grow with practice, so today's wobble is not a fixed trait. The word yet captures this: I can't ride my bike yet.

Common mistakes: praising persistence that is really repetition, when a child tries the same thing ten times and gets more upset; treating a break as quitting, when a short calm break is often what lets a child return; praising being clever, which can make children avoid hard tasks so they keep the label; and comparing with a sibling or friend who learned faster. Research on mindset messages shows small average effects, so the daily habits matter more than slogans.

At home, choose something just a little too hard, such as a jigsaw, a skipping rope or a tricky word. When your child makes a mistake, ask what it tells them to change. Notice effort and new strategies out loud: you tried a different way that time. Let them see you get something wrong and try again.

familyTip: When your child says "I can't do it", add "yet" together, then ask "What could you try differently?" Praise the new try, not just the result.

practice.prompt: Mo throws a ball at a target. It lands {n} steps too short. What should Mo try next?
choices: stop and say he is bad at throwing
practice.hint: Too short is a clue. What change would make the ball go further?
practice.explain: The ball fell {n} steps short, so the clue says throw a bit harder. The same throw would land in the same place.

practice.prompt: Which thought helps you keep trying?
choices: It is too hard for me.
practice.hint: Look for the little word that means you will get there.
practice.explain: The word yet means you are still learning. The other two make you want to stop.

practice.prompt: Lily practised her bike for {n} days. On day 1 she fell a lot. What most likely happened?
choices: she got steadier as she practised
she fell just as much every day
practice.hint: Think of Pip's wobbles in the lab. What happened to them each day of practice?
practice.explain: With {n} days of practice, Lily got steadier. Practice makes hard things easier.

practice.prompt: Kit's block tower fell down three times. Kit feels very cross. What is the best thing to do?
choices: take a calm break, then try a new way
practice.hint: Is a short break the same as giving up?
practice.explain: A calm break helps Kit think again. Then a new way, like big blocks at the bottom, can work.

pool.prompt: You get a word wrong in your spelling. What does the mistake tell you?
choices: that you are bad at spelling
that you should hide your work
pool.hint: A mistake is a clue. What is it a clue about?
pool.explain: A mistake shows you which part to fix. Everyone makes mistakes when they learn.

pool.prompt: Ben has tried a puzzle the same way {n} times and it still does not work. What should he do?
pool.hint: What happened in the lab when Pip threw with the same power twice?
pool.explain: Ben tried the same way {n} times. The same try gives the same result, so he should change something.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a break, not giving up?
choices: I'll have a drink and come back to it.
I'll say I finished when I didn't.
pool.hint: A break has a plan to come back.
pool.explain: Having a drink and coming back is a break. The other two stop the learning.

pool.prompt: Your friend can already tie her laces. You can't yet. What is true?
choices: people learn things at different speeds
your friend is cleverer at everything
pool.hint: Did Pip ride the bike on day 1?
pool.explain: People learn at different speeds. With practice you will get there too.

pool.prompt: Ava wants to hop on one foot for {n} hops. Today she can only do 2. What will help most?
choices: give up: some kids just can't hop
pool.hint: How did the wobbles change when Pip practised each day?
pool.explain: Practising a little every day will help Ava get closer to {n} hops.

pool.prompt: Which word turns "I can't read this" into a keep-going thought?
pool.hint: Which word means you are still learning it?
pool.explain: "I can't read this yet" means you are learning and will get there.

pool.prompt: Sam tried three different ways and is still stuck after a long time. What now?
choices: ask for a clue, then keep going
ask someone to do it for him
pool.hint: Keeping going does not mean doing it all alone. What kind of help still lets Sam learn?
pool.explain: After trying different ways, a clue helps Sam keep going and finish it himself.

pool.prompt: What does it mean when something feels hard?
pool.hint: Was riding a bike hard for Pip at first? Is it still hard after practice?
pool.explain: Hard means you are learning something new. It gets easier with practice.

visual.caption: Is it a break, or giving up? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: I'll have a drink and come back.
I'll rest, then try a new way.
I'll put it in the bin.
I'll say I'm done when I'm not.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: use each miss as a clue, practise day by day, pick keep-going thoughts, and take a break before trying a new way.
